Without government protection against competition in the form of medicinal copyright law, he'd be forced to charge significantly lower prices.

It's patent law - not copyright. Patents, copyrights, and trademarks are all intellectual property (IP) protection concepts but all very different in their terms, scope, and rules. In this case what you're suggesting is really not considering the pharmaceutical or an increasing number of high tech industries. Medical research involves spending billions of dollars in research and development to finally create an end product that costs almost nothing to produce and can be trivially reverse engineered. In a world where there was no form of IP protection it would be impossible to develop commercially develop pharmaceuticals. You spend a billion dollars developing your latest drug. It gets knocked off after a couple of weeks on the market, when you haven't even yet recouped a fraction of your costs, and sold for $0.10 a pill.

This problem is not unique to pharmaceuticals. Any field where the vast majority of costs come in the creation of a product that can be trivially replicated and costs relatively little to product face similar issues. For instance every single digital product, written works, etc.

You're definitely right patent law is being horrifically abused, but trying to entirely get rid of it is throwing the baby out with the bathwater. Complete laissez-faire economics only really works in relatively primitive markets where the majority of products sold have the majority of their costs tangibly tied to the physical product itself. As 3D technology printing continues to evolve, you'll begin to see this sort of economic problem start to reach even to physical goods. Keeping capitalism working when dealing with modern technology and products unfortunately entails some form of IP protection. It's a matter of keeping that protection reasonable and fair, which it currently is not.
